condition: Mixed Malaria (P. falciparum + P. vivax) - severe/critical
presentingComplaint: High-grade fever with chills for 6 days, now drowsy with reduced urine output and yellowish discolouration of eyes for 1 day
history: Migrant construction labourer who returned 10 days ago from a forested district of Odisha (eastern India). Fever was initially intermittent with rigors and drenching sweats every 36-48 hours, self-medicated with paracetamol and an unspecified oral antimalarial for 2 days without relief. Over the last 24 hours the family noted increasing lethargy, confused speech, dark 'tea-coloured' urine and progressively reduced urine output. No prior comorbidities, not on regular medication, no alcohol use. No recent surgery or catheterisation. This is not the classic single-species uncomplicated presentation - he has crossed into multi-organ dysfunction (cerebral, renal, hepatic, haematological) which mandates management as severe malaria irrespective of parasite density.
examination: Ill and toxic-looking, drowsy (GCS 13, E3V4M6), icteric sclerae, moderate pallor. Mildly dehydrated with dry mucosae. Soft splenomegaly (spleen palpable 3 cm below costal margin) and mild tender hepatomegaly. No neck stiffness, no focal neurological deficit, plantars flexor. No rash, no eschar, no lymphadenopathy. Chest clear; mild bibasal crepitations. Abdomen soft, non-peritonitic.

labs.parasiteIndex: P. falciparum ring forms ~6% parasitised RBCs

imaging: Chest X-ray: early bilateral lower-zone haziness suggestive of evolving ARDS/pulmonary oedema. USG abdomen: splenomegaly with mild hepatomegaly, no biliary dilatation, no abscess.
microbiology: Peripheral blood smear (thick and thin, Giemsa): dual infection confirmed - P. falciparum ring forms with occasional banana-shaped gametocytes AND P. vivax trophozoites with Schüffner's dots in enlarged infected RBCs. Rapid diagnostic test positive for both HRP-2 (P. falciparum) and pan-Plasmodium (pLDH) antigens. Blood cultures sterile at 48h. Dengue NS1/IgM negative, leptospira IgM negative, Widal non-diagnostic.
finalDiagnosis: Severe mixed-species malaria (P. falciparum + P. vivax) with cerebral involvement, acute kidney injury, hyperbilirubinaemia, severe thrombocytopenia, hyperlactataemia and hypoglycaemia
citations: WHO - Guidelines for Malaria (Severe Malaria management, IV artesunate) - 2023
NVBDCP/NCVBDC India - National Guidelines for Diagnosis and Treatment of Malaria - 2014
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Malaria
stewardship: Manage as severe falciparum malaria (mixed infection): immediate IV artesunate 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12 and 24h then daily, with parenteral therapy for ≥24h until able to tolerate oral. Follow with a full oral ACT course (artemether-lumefantrine) plus, after G6PD testing, primaquine 0.25 mg/kg/day for 14 days for anti-relapse radical cure of the P. vivax hypnozoite component. Supportive care: correct hypoglycaemia, judicious fluids, monitor for ARDS/renal replacement, treat as ICU-level severe malaria.
contraindications: Avoid oral-only antimalarials in severe disease - parenteral artesunate is mandatory
Do NOT give primaquine before excluding G6PD deficiency (haemolysis risk)
Avoid aggressive fluid boluses given ARDS risk in severe malaria
Avoid empirical steroids for cerebral malaria (proven harmful)
edgeCases: Low P. vivax parasitaemia can be masked by dominant falciparum on smear - always report species-level
Severe disease may occur even at relatively low parasite counts in non-immune adults
Hypoglycaemia may be worsened by quinine if used instead of artesunate
Delayed post-artesunate haemolytic anaemia can occur ~1-3 weeks later - monitor Hb
expectedMaiK: Severe malaria is a medical emergency defined by organ dysfunction (impaired consciousness, AKI, jaundice, acidosis/hyperlactataemia, hypoglycaemia, severe anaemia, ARDS) plus asexual parasitaemia; a positive smear/RDT with any WHO severity criterion mandates IV artesunate regardless of species, and confirmed mixed P. falciparum + P. vivax additionally requires anti-relapse radical cure with primaquine after G6PD testing.
expectedNextQuestions: Detailed travel/residence history in endemic/forested areas and timing
Any prior antimalarial self-medication or incomplete treatment
G6PD status and prior haemolytic episodes
Assess consciousness serially (GCS) and check capillary glucose
expectedInvestigations: Peripheral blood smear (thick + thin) for species and parasite density
Renal function, electrolytes, liver function, bilirubin
Blood cultures and dengue/lepto/scrub serology to exclude mimics

investigations: Peripheral blood smear (thick + thin) with species identification
Renal and liver function with bilirubin

regressionAssertions: Must identify MIXED_MALARIA as the leading diagnosis given dual-species smear/RDT positivity
Must recognise WHO severe-malaria criteria (cerebral involvement, AKI, jaundice, hyperlactataemia, hypoglycaemia) and escalate to IV artesunate
Must not downgrade to oral-only therapy despite modest parasite density
Must flag primaquine radical cure for the P. vivax component contingent on G6PD status
Must retain DENGUE and LEPTOSPIROSIS as reasonable mimics but exclude them via negative serology
